title: What If a Tsunami Hit Your Beach Vacation?
description:
A tsunami hits your beach vacation, and the only way out is up.
At 4:12 PM the wave comes over the pool deck. Theo, the lifeguard, pulls you into the hotel elevator with a little girl named Ava, and then the sea comes in after you.

0:00 The Wave (4:12 PM)
0:35 Rule 1: Never Take the Elevator
1:26 Rule 2: Never Jump In After Someone
2:21 Rule 3: The Higher, the Better
2:49 Rule 4: When the Sea Pulls Back, Run
4:21 Rule 5: The First Wave Isn't the Biggest
6:09 Rule 6: Never Push a Door That Opens In
7:34 Rule 7: Pick a Meeting Place

Subscribe for the next story.

The story is made up. The safety facts in it are real:
• Never use an elevator in an emergency; when the power goes, it stops where it is (NFPA, Ready.gov)
• Most elevator roof hatches lock from the outside, so passengers can't climb into the shaft (ASME A17.1 elevator safety code)
• Elevators aren't watertight; floodwater gets in at the doors (elevator industry flood guidance)
• Every elevator must have an emergency phone (ASME A17.1)
• Elevators don't free-fall: a safety brake grips the rails if a car drops (ASME A17.1 car safeties)
• Elevator glass is laminated, so it cracks but holds together (ASME A17.1)
• Water pushes on glass harder the deeper it is (hydrostatic pressure)
• Never jump in after someone in moving water: reach, throw, row, go (American Red Cross)
• Holding something that floats keeps you alive in moving water (NOAA, National Weather Service)
• When you can't get out, go up: the third floor or higher of a reinforced concrete building, the higher the better (FEMA P-646, vertical evacuation)
• When the sea suddenly pulls back from a beach, a tsunami is minutes away (NOAA, International Tsunami Information Center)
• The water running back out is as dangerous as the wave coming in, and much of the harm is the debris it carries (NOAA, National Weather Service)
• Near the shore a tsunami still moves at about 20 to 30 mph, faster than anyone can run (NOAA)
• A tsunami comes in like a tide that won't stop rising, not like a breaking surf wave (NOAA, National Weather Service)
• The first wave of a tsunami is often not the biggest, and waves keep coming for hours (NOAA, National Weather Service)
• Six inches of moving water can knock an adult down (National Weather Service, Turn Around Don't Drown)
• In many tall buildings, stair doors lock from the stairwell side, with re-entry only on some floors (NFPA 101, International Building Code)
• Big exit doors must swing outward, because a crowd pushing on a door that opens toward it holds it shut (NFPA 101 Life Safety Code)
• In a crowd crush, the people at the front can't step back; the push comes from behind (crowd safety research, G. Keith Still)
• Families who pick a meeting place before a disaster find each other faster (FEMA, Ready.gov "Make a Plan")

title: Fog Apocalypse: I Survived 90 Days Inside the Deadly Fog (Full Movie)
description:
Fog Apocalypse: I Survived 90 Days Inside the Deadly Fog (Full Movie)

The complete Fog Apocalypse story in one video: all 90 days, from the first knock on the door to the last night in Dry Creek. No waiting for the next part.

It starts on an ordinary Tuesday at 5:58 PM. A wall of fog rolls over the hills, and by 11 PM something outside is knocking on your door, speaking in your mom's voice. The fog is alive. It copies voices. And every single day, it arrives 10 minutes earlier.

With only your little sister Lily, a set of rules written on the fridge, and a clock that never stops shrinking, you have to cross a dead country: from your sealed house, to a water plant lit by UV lamps, across 200 miles on a bike with a homemade lamp and a stray dog named Chain, to a tiny desert town where the fog has learned to hide in the water.

One family. Six rules. Ninety days. This is the full movie.

title: What if You Could See Everyone's Real-Life Rating? Part3
description:
One morning my player card turns gold. Ninety-nine. Pace, passing, everything.

I outrun the bus. I score from the halfway line. Half of Year Nine wants a selfie. But every time I score, something tiny floats off my teammates' heads. Minus one. Minus one.

Then I read the stat at the bottom of my card. And I find out where my ninety-nine came from.

Real-Life Rating, Part 3.

If you could be a ninety-nine, but every point came from your friends, would you keep it? Tell me in the comments.

title: What If You Could See Everyone's Potential?
description:
What if you could see everyone's potential? I discovered a way to view the hidden talent rating of every student around me.

Two numbers float above every person's head. The white figure represents their current status, while the gold number reveals the absolute best they could ever be. I started tracking these stats at school, watching as a player with a modest eighty-five rating revealed a gold ninety-eight. My own rating was a solid ninety-nine, until the morning it suddenly changed.

Everything rests on the upcoming county trials. With only one place available, I am forced to decide if a person's worth is defined by their current performance or their future promise. This animated story follows my struggle to determine whose dream deserves the final spot, and whether seeing the truth about someone is a gift or a heavy burden.

If you could see your own potential, would you want to know the number? Tell me in the comments, and subscribe for new animated stories every week.

title: What If You Could STOP Time for Everyone But You?
description:
What if you could STOP time for everyone but you? ⏸️⏳ One snap of your fingers in the middle of a math test, and the whole world freezes. The clock. Your teacher. Even the fly in front of your face.

At first, you use it for pranks. Then you realize you could use it for something way bigger. You train in the frozen gym, read every book in the library, and build something that changes your family's life forever. Strong. Smart. Rich. But every hour in frozen time comes with a cost nobody else can see.

What would YOU master first if you could stop time? Would you use it to get ahead, or to help the people around you?

If you enjoyed this story, watch our other videos:
🧠 What If You Could Hear Everyone's Thoughts?

What's the first thing you'd do with one frozen hour? Tell us in the comments, and subscribe for more animated what-if stories! ⏱️

title: What If Humans Never Discovered Clothes?
tags: what if humans never discovered clothes
description:
What if humans never discovered clothes? We examine a world stripped of textiles to see how our survival relies on ingenuity.

This animation explores the absence of human inventions like bandages and fabric in a harsh environment. By visualizing a landscape where our ancestors lacked basic warmth, we illustrate how the development of protective layers fundamentally shifted our species from vulnerable beings to masters of diverse climates.

Without the ability to create shelter or clothing, humanity would have remained confined to limited regions. This thought experiment highlights how simple items we take for granted are the true pillars of civilization. Understanding the impact of prehistoric technology shows us why these simple innovations were the turning point for our survival.

If you were born in a world without any protection from the elements, how would you adapt? Tell us in the comments.

description:
One morning, a glowing red heart appears above everyone's head, and inside it is a wedding photo of the person they're going to marry. Then you see the heart above Sophie. And the boy in her future is Noah, the quiet kid that Brandon, the most popular guy in school, picks on every single day.

So you decide to help fate along. A design competition, a tiny model house, and a matchmaking plan that's supposed to be perfect, until Brandon finds out. As the hearts start to flicker and change, you learn that the future isn't something you can just see. It's something people choose. And six years later, at a wedding in a garden, your own heart has one last surprise for you.

title: What If You Could Read Everyone's LAST Text Message?
description:
The lunch lady is one nugget request away from moving to Canada. Your best friend is begging strangers for the bio answers. The most popular senior in school is filming a video about living without his phone while it sits at two percent. You know all of this because everyone's last text floats over their head in a little grey bubble, with a tiny timestamp underneath, and nobody else can see a single one. Yours never shows up. Not even in a mirror.

By Tuesday your friend Mateo has turned it into a five-dollar business. By Wednesday the whole school is sure you hack phones, the vice principal has yours sealed in a ziploc bag, and the only person not sliding her desk away is Sloane, the girl across the aisle in English, who works you out with three test texts. Then she takes you to her nana's house. Over the old woman's head sits one bubble that hasn't moved in twenty-six days. On Saturday it finally changes, and it's the last thing you wanted to read.

If you could read just one person's bubble for the rest of your life — your crush, your teacher, or your grandparents — whose would you pick?

0:34 Two percent battery
2:12 Ask the Hoodie, five bucks a question
3:20 A rumor with timestamps

5:54 A bubble that never moves
7:35 Nine thousand for a new roof
9:43 Eight minutes to noon
12:06 The driveway
13:19 One text of your own

Real things hiding in this story
• The first text message ever was "Merry Christmas," typed on a computer by engineer Neil Papworth on 3 December 1992 and received on an Orbitel 901 phone. That phone could not send anything back (History.com, NPR).
• MIT researchers followed about 126,000 stories on Twitter. False ones reached people roughly six times faster than true ones (Vosoughi, Roy & Aral, Science, 2018).
• In McAfee's 2023 voice-cloning tests, a clip of about three seconds was enough to produce an 85% voice match.
• The "grandparent scam" is a real FBI term: a fake grandchild in trouble, a fake lawyer, a courier at the door for cash. In the FBI's 2024 report, people over 60 reported close to $4.9 billion in losses to fraud (IC3 2024).
• In December 2024 the FBI advised families to agree on a secret word or phrase to check that a voice on the phone is really theirs (IC3 PSA I-120324).

Mateo, Wade, Sloane and Nana Lois are made up, and nobody is reading the bubble over your head. But if your grandparents have never heard of a family code word, tonight is a good night to pick one.
